record.text: JMIR Res Protocols: Interventions to Support Healthy Movement Behaviors Among Preschool Children in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: #Protocol for a Realist Synthesis

external.description: Background: A paradigm shift toward a broader view of movement behaviors emphasizes the importance of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep across the 24-hour day. Despite these behaviors being positively associated with important health and development outcomes, #Research suggests that many preschool children worldwide fail to meet the World Health Organization 24-hour movement behavior guidelines. To improve adherence, interventions have often targeted early childhood education and care settings, key environments where children spend a substantial proportion of their day. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of these interventions and their components is inconsistent. These inconsistencies highlight the complexity of movement behavior interventions, as movement behaviors are interdependent and influenced by multiple contextual factors. Considering this, a theory-driven approach is best suited to develop a deeper understanding of what works for whom, under which circumstances, and how, ultimately improving policy and intervention development. Objective: The aim of this #Protocol is to investigate under which contextual circumstances interventions most effectively improve preschool children’s 24-hour movement behaviors in early childhood education and care settings by developing an evidence-informed initial program theory that outlines for whom these interventions work, under what contexts, and through which mechanisms. Methods: Findings from the synthesis will be reported in accordance with the RAMESES (Realist and Meta-Narrative Evidence Synthesis: Evolving Standards) publication standards. A literature search will be conducted to identify relevant peer-reviewed movement behavior intervention studies. Identified studies will be considered for inclusion based on predetermined inclusion criteria. #Study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment will be independently conducted by 2 reviewers. The realist synthesis will apply a combined conceptual framework to develop potential context-mechanism-outcome configurations and an initial program theory, which will be refined—through piecemeal confirmation and/or disconfirmation—during the evidence synthesis. Results: Duplicate screening, quality assessment, data extraction, relevance and rigor appraisal, and iterative program theory testing are planned for completion by the end of 2026. The primary review manuscript is targeted for submission by early 2027. Conclusions: This review shifts away from the current literature’s focus on intervention effectiveness and instead develops a more nuanced understanding of intervention implementation and effectiveness by applying theory-driven processes. The results of the synthesis intend to identify appropriate strategies to promote healthy 24-hour movement behaviors in the early years to inform the development, adaptation, and implementation of current and future interventions. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261449684; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261449684

record.text: New JMIR MedInform: The IDEA Framework for Clinician-Led Data Curation in a Hospital Clinical Data Warehouse: Single-Center Implementation Study

external.description: Background: Hospital clinical data warehouses (CDWs) contain longitudinal #patient-level information distributed across heterogeneous clinical domains and require strict governance, privacy protection, and controlled data access. Although disease-specific registries facilitate structured clinical #research, routine hospital CDW workflows often require repeated technical intervention when clinicians iteratively refine cohorts or integrate additional variables. At Samsung #medical Center (Seoul, Republic of Korea), an operational audit revealed a mean turnaround time of 2.7 (SD 1.6) weeks for clinical data extraction requests, highlighting a workflow gap between clinicians’ #research questions and engineer-mediated database query development. Objective: This study describes the development and single-center implementation of IDEA (intersection, difference, expansion, attribution), an #informatics abstraction framework designed to support authorized clinicians in performing iterative cohort construction and variable integration within a governed hospital CDW. Methods: IDEA implements 4 user-facing operations: intersection (I), difference (D), expansion (E), and attribution (A). Attribution enables dynamic integration of variables from multiple predefined clinical data domains into an active cohort. IDEA was implemented within the Samsung #medical Center CDW, containing longitudinal #ehrs from 1995 to 2025 and 12 cancer registries. The implementation was evaluated using oncology cross-registry scenarios, descriptive analysis of user actions recorded between January 2024 and December 2025, including 11,460 IDEA operator events, and analysis of 349 user-defined cohorts (“My Registries”) established from 2022 to 2025. Results: IDEA supported interactive cohort construction, refinement, and attribute-based stratification across 12 cancer registries without manual SQL authoring. Clinical end users generated the majority of the 11,460 operator interactions: #research nurses accounted for 7918 (69.1%), physicians for 2871 (25.1%), and IT personnel for 619 (5.4%). Attribution was the most frequent operation (8726, 76.1%), suggesting that iterative variable integration into established cohorts was a major use case. Additionally, 349 user-defined cohorts were registered as reusable baseline populations for subsequent cohort curation. Conclusions: IDEA serves as a complementary pathway for clinician-led data curation within a governed hospital CDW, integrating cohort refinement, variable integration, and reusable cohort management into a single workflow. This approach may support selected routine curation tasks for authorized users working with quality-validated data, while complex requests continue to require analyst support. Multicenter evaluations are needed to independently assess dataset accuracy, completeness, and institutional transferability.
